title: India Approves Record $13.3 Billion Semiconductor Package as Tata and Micron Fabs Take Shape
excerpt: The Semicon 2.0 programme marks India's largest chip funding push, with three facilities already in commercial production and Tata's Dholera fab preparing for first silicon.
body:
• India's cabinet approved a ₹1.28 trillion ($13.3 billion) Semicon 2.0 programme on July 15, the largest semiconductor funding package in the country's history.
  • Tata Electronics will begin chip production at its Dholera fab with 90nm process technology before scaling to 28nm nodes, in partnership with Taiwan's PSMC.
  • Micron, Kaynes and CG Semi have started commercial production at their Indian facilities, with more plants expected to come online in 2026.
  • The government has identified 105 chip design startups and expects at least 50 deep-tech companies to emerge under ISM 2.0's focus on design IP and R&D.

India's Biggest Semiconductor Bet Yet

India approved ₹1.28 trillion ($13.3 billion) in fresh funding for its semiconductor programme on July 15, according to Information Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw. The package, known as Semicon 2.0, marks a decisive shift from the first phase's emphasis on building fabrication plants to a broader strategy encompassing chip design, intellectual property creation and AI-ready chip development.

Alongside the semiconductor allocation, the cabinet also approved ₹625 billion for mobile phone manufacturing, underscoring the government's push to make India a global electronics hub.

Fabs Moving From Blueprint to Production

The physical infrastructure is taking shape across Gujarat. Three companies — Micron Technology, Kaynes and CG Semi — have already started commercial production at their Indian facilities. Micron's $2.75 billion Assembly, Test, Marking and Packaging plant in Sanand completed Phase 1, validating high-spec cleanrooms and ramping toward high-volume DRAM and NAND memory production.

Tata Electronics, meanwhile, is preparing to fire up India's first large-scale fabrication plant in the Dholera Special Investment Region. Built in partnership with Taiwan's Powerchip Semiconductor Manufacturing Corp., the facility will begin with 90nm process technology before progressing to 28nm — the "workhorse" nodes used in automotive electronics, 5G infrastructure and power management chips.

"In semiconductors, the supply chain must move at the speed of light. Proximity matters. Local presence and local end-support and services matter."

— Sanjay Mehrotra, CEO, Micron Technology

CG Semi, in partnership with Renesas Electronics, plans to scale its Sanand OSAT facility to roughly 4 billion chips annually by the time a second plant opens in 2027.

ISM 2.0: From Building Fabs to Owning the Brains

Where the first phase of India's semiconductor mission focused on factory construction, ISM 2.0 pivots toward high-value chip design and R&D. The government has approved 24 semiconductor design projects from startups and MSMEs and granted 105 companies access to industry-standard Electronic Design Automation tools. These firms are designing chips for satellite communications, drones, AI systems, telecom equipment and IoT devices.

The emerging startup ecosystem includes Agrani, which is developing India's first indigenous GPUs to reduce reliance on Western hardware for AI training, and C2I, which is building specialized power-management chips for data centres. Semiconductor startup funding has grown tenfold, from $5 million in 2023 to $50 million in 2025, though industry leaders say far more capital is needed.

"The idea of co-investment is two-fold," S. Krishnan, Secretary at the Ministry of Electronics and IT, told PTI. "One, that we increase the overall funding. Two, the government doesn't do the selection. When whitelisted venture capitalist funds invest, we will co-invest."

What It Means for NRIs in Tech

India's semiconductor push is creating opportunities that could accelerate reverse brain drain. The sector needs tens of thousands of skilled engineers for roles spanning chip design, process engineering and manufacturing intelligence. Indian-origin executives already hold senior positions at global chipmakers, and the expanding domestic ecosystem could offer compelling reasons to return.

The Road Ahead

The next 18 months are critical. Tata's Dholera fab must achieve target yields at its initial nodes, Micron's Sanand plant needs to hit high-volume export targets, and the 105 design startups must transition from tape-outs to revenue. Industry analysts project that India could account for nearly 10% of global semiconductor production capacity by 2030 if execution keeps pace with ambition.

ISM 2.0 also extends into compound semiconductors like silicon carbide and gallium nitride, materials essential for next-generation electric vehicles and 6G telecommunications. The question, as Endiya Partners' Sateesh Andra put it, "has shifted from 'will we build fabs?' to 'can we operate them competitively?'"
